stem:
A Form 3 class studied a granite area on the plateau of southern Zimbabwe. They recorded the climate at a nearby station (fictional data, Table 1) and described the landforms they saw.

Table 1: climate at the station.

| Month | January | April | July | October |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mean daily maximum temperature (°C) | 28 | 26 | 23 | 32 |
| Mean daily minimum temperature (°C) | 16 | 12 | 6 | 13 |
| Mean monthly rainfall (mm) | 150 | 30 | 2 | 25 |

Field notes: 'Large bare domes of smooth rock with curved sheets peeling off their surfaces. Piles of rounded boulders on low hills. In places one boulder rests on another at a tiny point of contact. Some hills are made of square blocks stacked like walls. Sandy soils with red colouring between the hills.'

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Granite belongs to which group of rocks?

options.rationale: Correct: magma cooled slowly underground, giving large crystals.
Extrusive rocks such as basalt cool at the surface and have small crystals.
Sedimentary rocks are laid down in layers from sediment.
Metamorphic rocks are changed by heat and pressure; granite crystallised from magma.

parts.explanation: Granite is an intrusive (plutonic) igneous rock.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean daily temperature range for the four months shown. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the month in Table 1 when conditions most favour chemical weathering.
parts.explanation: January is both warm and wet (150 mm), so reactions such as hydrolysis are fastest.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why chemical weathering of granite is faster in January than in July.

points.description: January is wet (150 mm) while July is almost dry (2 mm)
Hydrolysis needs water to react with feldspar, turning it into clay
January is warmer (mean maximum 28 °C compared with 23 °C)
Higher temperatures speed up chemical reactions

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In January the station receives 150 mm of rain but in July only 2 mm. Hydrolysis needs water to react with the feldspar in granite and turn it into clay, so it can only work well in the wet season. January is also warmer (28 °C maximum against 23 °C), and chemical reactions are faster at higher temperatures.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Match each landform in the field notes to its name.

left.content: Large bare dome of smooth rock with curved sheets peeling off
One boulder resting on another at a tiny point of contact

parts.explanation: Dwalas have few joints; balancing rocks are corestones left perched; castle kopjes form where vertical and horizontal joints cross.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe the formation of the piles of rounded boulders (kopjes) mentioned in the field notes. You may describe a sequence of diagrams in words.

points.description: Granite is cut by joints, some closely spaced and some widely spaced
Water moves down joints; chemical weathering (hydrolysis) rots the granite below the surface
Where joints are widely spaced, solid rounded corestones remain within the weathered regolith
The regolith is removed by rain and running water, exposing the corestones as a kopje

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Granite has joints at different spacings. Water seeps down the joints and hydrolysis rots the rock below ground, producing a deep regolith of clay and sand. Where joints are far apart, solid blocks survive and are rounded into corestones. Over a long time rain and streams wash the regolith away, leaving the corestones piled on solid rock as a kopje.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Complete the sentences about physical weathering in the granite area.

payload.template: The curved sheets peeling off the domes are caused by {{blank:a}}. Grains loosening because dark and light minerals expand by different amounts is called {{blank:b}} disintegration.

parts.explanation: Exfoliation (with pressure release) forms the curved sheets; granular disintegration loosens individual grains.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: With reference to a named granite area of Zimbabwe, explain how weathering has shaped the landscape and evaluate the value of this landscape to people.

points.description: Named area, e.g. Matobo Hills / Epworth / Domboshava / Masvingo district
Chemical weathering along joints (hydrolysis) and stripping produce kopjes and balancing rocks
Exfoliation and pressure release produce dwalas; joint pattern explains castle kopjes
Weathered granite gives sandy, often infertile soils between the hills
Value: tourism and heritage (e.g. Matobo World Heritage Site, rock art, Epworth balancing rocks)
Value: building stone and quarrying, water catchment and small dams between hills
Limitations: thin sandy soils limit farming; steep bare rock unusable for crops; quarrying damages scenery

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The Matobo Hills south of Bulawayo are a granite landscape shaped by weathering. Water moving down joints rotted the granite by hydrolysis below the surface; where joints were widely spaced, corestones survived and, once the regolith was stripped away, they were left as kopjes and balancing rocks. Large unjointed masses shed curved sheets by exfoliation and pressure release, forming dwalas, while crossing joints produced castle kopjes. Between the hills the weathered granite gives sandy soils. The landscape is valuable: the Matobo Hills are a World Heritage Site with rock art and wildlife, attracting tourists; granite is quarried for building stone; and rain running off bare rock fills small dams. However, the sandy soils are low in nutrients, the bare rock cannot be farmed, and quarrying can spoil the scenery. Overall the landscape is more valuable for tourism, heritage and water than for farming, so careful protection brings the greatest benefit.

explanation: The question links rocks, weathering processes and granite landforms to a Zimbabwean landscape, as in ZIMSEC Paper 2 Section A.
hints: Link each landform in the field notes to joint spacing and a weathering process.
